content: # Decoding B1479 on the 2011 Lexus RX350: Sensor Location and Replacement Strategy When a diagnostic scanner returns DTC B1479 on a 2011 Lexus RX350, the immediate symptom is usually a complete loss of cooling. The system logic interprets this specific code as a fault within the A/C Pressure Sensor Switch circuit. While the error indicates a failure in the pressure sensing loop, determining the physical location of the faulty component often leads to conflicting information online. Some forums suggest the sensor is an integral part of the AC compressor assembly, implying that replacing the sensor requires removing the entire compressor unit. However, official OEM documentation from Lexus parts catalogs presents a different picture. The parts list explicitly categorizes "SENSOR--AIR-CONDITIONER-PRESSURE" as a standalone replaceable item rather than a sealed component within the compressor drive. This distinction is critical for cost-benefit analysis before initiating repairs. If the sensor were truly built into the compressor housing, it would be listed only under the compressor part number. The fact that a dedicated pressure sensor exists in the parts hierarchy suggests a modular design where the sensing element can be serviced independently of the mechanical pump. To verify which scenario applies to your specific vehicle, physical inspection is non-negotiable. The provided image typically highlights the location of the pressure sensor on the high-pressure side of the refrigerant loop. In most RX350 configurations, this sensor is mounted directly onto the liquid line or the accumulator/drier assembly, not inside the compressor casing itself. When looking at the component pointed to by the red arrow in standard diagrams, you are observing the external pressure transducer. If your unit matches this visual reference, the "built-in" theory is incorrect for that specific setup. The technical implication of this distinction is significant regarding repair strategy. Swapping the entire AC compressor on a 2011 RX350 involves evacuating the system, replacing the oil charge, and recharging with R-134a refrigerant. This process introduces risk: compressors are delicate components, and improper handling can lead to internal damage or seal failure. Furthermore, if the original issue was indeed a failed pressure sensor rather than mechanical wear in the compressor, swapping the whole unit is an unnecessary expense that could cost several hundred dollars more than required. Before committing to a compressor replacement, you should inspect the standalone sensor for physical damage, corrosion on the electrical connector, or signs of refrigerant leakage at the mounting point. If the sensor is accessible and separate from the compressor, replacing it is the logical first step. This approach minimizes labor hours and reduces the risk of introducing new failures into the cooling system. If you are managing a fleet of vehicles or dealing with multiple units exhibiting similar symptoms, accurate parts identification prevents budget overruns. Always cross-reference the VIN-specific parts availability to confirm whether your vehicle utilizes the integrated sensor design or the standalone unit. Relying on anecdotal forum posts without verifying against official OEM diagrams can lead to expensive mistakes. For those looking for further validation on part compatibility or specific repair procedures, resources like LaravelCompany often provide structured guides on automotive diagnostics and parts identification, though direct consultation with a certified technician remains the safest path for complex HVAC systems. The goal is to resolve the B1479 error by addressing the actual hardware fault, not by swapping entire assemblies based on ambiguous online claims.
